title: Satire in ancient Kashmir
description: The book Three Satires from Ancient Kashmir takes the reader back to the times when Kashmir was demographically Hindu. When this book was written for the first time in Sanskrit, the advent of Islam was still two to three centuries away in time. Although, some historical accounts suggest that Islam had made its entry into Kashmir way before 14th century when Islam marked a major advance into the valley. The book is a voyage through the cultural landscape of the ancient Kashmir. Rather it is more accurate to say that the book sketches the landscape of Kashmir when the west wind of Islam was round the corner. In any case, there is no mention of the transition to a new demography in the Three Satires from Ancient Kashmir. Translated from Sanskrit to English by A.N.D. Haksar, a veteran writer in the field of translation work from Sanskrit to English. A career diplomat who has served in the diplomatic circles as the Indian High Commissioner to Kenya and the Seychelles, and ambassador to Portugal and Yugoslavia. He has previously translated works from Sanskrit to English. Three Satires from Ancient Kashmir brings to the contemporary audience the everyday life of the eleventh century Kashmir. Originally, written by Kshemendra in the 11th century, the three satires mentioned in the title of the book are: Narma Mala, or A Garland of Mirth, Kalavilasa, or A Dalliance with Deception and Desopadesa, or Advice from the Countryside. The translation of the three Sanskrit texts is based on the original as edited and published by the Osmania University, Hyderabad in 1961. The original manuscripts of Kshemendra, and also of other classical Sanskrit poeticians, were discovered by various European indologists from the late 19th century to early 20th century. Indologists like A.C. Burnell, G Buhler, A Stein, B. Peterson, S.C. Das and M.S. Kaul did a commendable service in identifying and locating the ancient manuscripts. The present, Three Satires from Ancient Kashmir, was discovered by A. C. Burnell at Tanjore in 1871. Essentially, the book casts all kinds of official, non-official and religious characters who are beset with moral and financial corruption. There is the government official, the clerk, the priest, the merchant, the widow, the astrologer, the village official, the courtesan with her retinue, the doctor, the local housewife. No one is spared the caustic satire. The characters are generally types, not merely isolated individuals. It seems the original purpose of the author was reform through the route of humorous satire. Although, the translation is scarcely able to evoke the humor. At many places the translator mentions in passing that Kshemendra wished to draws smiles from his audience. As, for example, in the epilogue of the Narma Mala, he says that these, ‘misdemeanors’ are narrated for the ‘recreation’ of people, and they also contain, ‘some fruitful counsel.’ But, as I said, one gets to know so many characters from that period of Kashmir, but there is hardly any scene that brings out the laughter. That is the pitfall of the translation. Not for nothing has someone said that translation is the reverse side of the carpet. However, it is true that the translator does succeed in informing today’s audience about the situation in the eleventh century Kashmir. Point to be noted is that the original is in poetry, as was most of the compositions in the ancient period. But the translator has rendered the translation in prose except some fragments towards the end of each satire. Truth be told, these fragments, the epilogues, are beautifully translated without changing the style of the original. That is why it us surprising as to why the translator did not retaining the original stylistic structure of the three satires. From the rendition of the epilogues of each of the three satires, it is without doubt that he would have produced a nice poetic translation of the original. Anyhow, Kshemendra has not spared anyone with his acerbic wit. The guru and the godman, the farmer and the father, the doctor and the bawd, all are held up for sarcastic view. Interestingly, the satires call to mind the 18th century english novel Joseph Andrews written by Henry Fielding. Also called the mock epic in prose, the 18th century text written in the form of a journey, holds up for view all kinds of people, who pretend to be what they are. There is the doctor, who behind his fake self is a charlatan. The lawyer knows anything except what he appears to be. Similarly, the Christian priest instead of being a good Samaritan is the last one to come to the help of the troubled Joseph. A woman who’s apparently mourning the death of her husband maneuvers the seduction of a young countryside boy. The descriptions in the Three Satires are not way too dissimilar to the ones sketched by Henry Fielding. The kings, systems and landscapes may be different, but the way the human character reveals itself is quite similar. It seems King Ananta, in whose time Kshemendra wrote the Three Satires was either incapable or helpless in controlling the situation described by Kshemendra. Country seems have to be submerged in decay and decadence, with little of exit from the a very despondent situation. Manipulation is rife while mannerisms are crooked. “Bow to the doctor. Devoid,” demonstrates Kshemendra the nature of the practitioner of medicine, “of knowledge and doer of dishonorable deeds, he strikes, like a serpent, many people with untimely death.” Centuries have passed, and it seems, not much has changed, although the inhabitants of Kashmir, like elsewhere in the world, are witness to bewildering technological transformations. If one reads the satirical poem of Zareef Ahmed Zareef, Tarangari (roughly translated as skullduggery), alongside this translation of Kshemendra’s book, it is not difficult to conclude that the more things change, the more they remain the same. What dissimilarities does one find in the tone and characters of the 21st century poem tarangari and the 11th century Sanskrit texts? Big conversion has occurred, yet, no big change is in place. Religion of the people has changed, yet the fundamental human character remained chiseled in rock. Three Satires from Ancient Kashmir appears to be a cry for reform. The rot is shown to have percolated down the political strata to the most intimate corners of the society. The noble and the ignoble are indistinguishable, and the high and the low all are infected by skullduggery and hypocrisy. What was done by the rulers and the lay who heard or read this book in the eleventh century one does not know, however, this much is clear that the writer like Kshemendra did not hesitate to expose the ills of the society without perhaps the fear of repercussions from those he held up for ridicule. Dr. Javaid Iqbal Bhat, Associate Professor, University of Kashmir, South Campus
